chapterTitle: Homes That Preach, Hearts Ready to Answer, and the Victorious Christ
themeTitle: “Always Be Ready to Give an Answer … Concerning the Hope That Is in You”

scripture.text: In the same way, wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; so that, even if any don’t obey the Word, they may be won by the behavior of their wives without a word;
scripture.understanding: ὁμοίως, “In the same way” — as with citizens (2:13) and servants (2:18), the pattern of Christ's suffering and trust (2:21–25) now shapes the home. γυναῖκες, ὑποτασσόμεναι τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν, “wives, be in subjection to your own husbands” — ὑποτάσσω, to rank oneself under, voluntary and ‘your own’, not every man. ἵνα καὶ εἴ τινες ἀπειθοῦσιν τῷ λόγῳ, “so that, even if any don’t obey the Word” — husbands who reject the gospel. διὰ τῆς τῶν γυναικῶν ἀναστροφῆς ἄνευ λόγου κερδηθήσονται, “they may be won by the behavior of their wives without a word” — a wordplay in the word family: those who refuse the λόγος (the message) may be won ἄνευ λόγου (without speech). κερδαίνω, to gain — the merchant's ‘make a profit’ of James 4:13, now used for winning a soul.

scripture.text: seeing your pure behavior in fear.
scripture.understanding: ἐποπτεύσαντες, “seeing” — ἐποπτεύω, from the see family: to watch closely as an eyewitness, the word used in 2:12 of unbelievers watching good works. τὴν ἐν φόβῳ ἁγνὴν ἀναστροφὴν ὑμῶν, “your pure behavior in fear” — ἁγνός, clean, chaste; φόβος, reverence towards God, not fear of the husband (v. 6). The unbelieving husband is watching.

scripture.text: Let your beauty be not just the outward adorning of braiding the hair, and of wearing jewels of gold, or of putting on fine clothing;
scripture.understanding: ὧν ἔστω οὐχ ὁ ἔξωθεν, “Let your beauty be not just the outward adorning” — ὁ … κόσμος: here κόσμος, from the world family, keeps its original meaning, ‘order, arrangement, adornment’ — the root of ‘cosmetic’. ἐμπλοκῆς τριχῶν, “of braiding the hair” — elaborate braided hairstyles woven with gold; περιθέσεως χρυσίων, “of wearing jewels of gold”; ἐνδύσεως ἱματίων, “of putting on fine clothing.” Peter does not forbid these; the WEB's ‘not just’ catches the sense: they must not be where beauty lies (1 Timothy 2:9).

scripture.text: but in the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God very precious.
scripture.understanding: ἀλλ᾽ ὁ κρυπτὸς τῆς καρδίας ἄνθρωπος, “but in the hidden person of the heart” — the inner self God sees. ἐν τῷ ἀφθάρτῳ, “in the incorruptible adornment” — ἄφθαρτος, imperishable, like the inheritance (1:4) and the seed (1:23); gold fades, this does not. τοῦ πραέος καὶ ἡσυχίου πνεύματος, “of a gentle and quiet spirit” — πραΰς, from the humble family: meek, strength under control, the word Jesus used of Himself (Matthew 11:29); ἡσύχιος, calm, settled, not anxious. ὅ ἐστιν ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ πολυτελές, “which is in the sight of God very precious” — πολυτελής, costly, the word used of the expensive perfume poured on Jesus (Mark 14:3).

scripture.text: For this is how the holy women before, who hoped in God also adorned themselves, being in subjection to their own husbands:
scripture.understanding: “For this is how the holy women before, who hoped in God also adorned themselves” — ἅγιαι, holy, set apart to God; ἐλπίζω, to hope, the living hope of 1:3; κοσμέω, the verb of the κόσμος of verse 3: to adorn, to put in order. Their beauty grew from their hope in God, not their fear of man.

scripture.text: as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord, whose children you now are, if you do well, and are not put in fear by any terror.
scripture.understanding: ὡς Σάρρα ὑπήκουσεν τῷ Ἀβραάμ, “as Sarah obeyed Abraham” — ὑπακούω, to listen and respond. κύριον αὐτὸν καλοῦσα, “calling him lord” — in Genesis 18:12 she says it to herself, a respectful word for ‘my husband’. ἧς ἐγενήθητε τέκνα, “whose children you now are” — Gentile women become daughters of Sarah by faith, as believers are children of Abraham. ἀγαθοποιοῦσαι, “if you do well” — ἀγαθοποιέω, from the good family, the ‘well-doing’ of 2:15, 20. καὶ μὴ φοβούμεναι μηδεμίαν πτόησιν, “and are not put in fear by any terror” — φοβέω and πτόησις, panic: submission is not fear-driven; it flows from trust in God (Proverbs 3:25). τέκνον is from the children family — a child — one born of a parent, family by birth.

scripture.text: You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman, as to the weaker vessel, as being also joint heirs of the grace of life; that your prayers may not be hindered.
scripture.understanding: οἱ ἄνδρες ὁμοίως, “You husbands, in the same way” — the same Christlike pattern binds husbands. συνοικοῦντες κατὰ γνῶσιν, “live with your wives according to knowledge” — γνῶσις, from the know family: understanding her, as distinct from ἐπίγνωσις, full knowledge of God. ἀπονέμοντες τιμήν, “giving honor” — τιμή, the honour of 2:17. ὡς ἀσθενεστέρῳ σκεύει τῷ γυναικείῳ, “to the woman, as to the weaker vessel” — σκεῦος, a vessel, a jar; ἀσθενής, weaker in physical strength and in social power, not in worth or spirit. ὡς καὶ συγκληρονόμοις χάριτος ζωῆς, “as being also joint heirs of the grace of life” — συγκληρονόμος, co-heir; ζωή, from the life family. ‘Weaker’ is immediately balanced by ‘equal heirs’. εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐγκόπτεσθαι τὰς προσευχὰς ὑμῶν, “that your prayers may not be hindered” — προσευχή, from the pray family; ἐγκόπτω, to cut into, as soldiers break up a road. A husband who dishonours his wife finds his prayers blocked.

scripture.text: Finally, be all like-minded, compassionate, loving as brothers, tender hearted, courteous,
scripture.understanding: τὸ δὲ τέλος, “Finally” — τέλος, from the perfect family: the goal, the sum of it all. Five qualities for the whole church: ὁμόφρονες, “like-minded” — one mind, the same direction; συμπαθεῖς, “compassionate” — from the mercy family: σύν + πάσχω, suffering with, feeling another's pain; φιλάδελφοι, “loving as brothers” — from the love family, the adjective of φιλαδελφία (1:22); εὔσπλαγχνοι, “tender hearted” — from the mercy family, compassion felt deep inside; φιλόφρονες, “courteous” — from the love family: friendly-minded. Many early manuscripts read ταπεινόφρονες instead, ‘humble-minded’, related to the ταπεινός of 5:5.

scripture.text: not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing; knowing that to this were you called, that you may inherit a blessing.
scripture.understanding: μὴ ἀποδιδόντες κακὸν ἀντὶ κακοῦ ἢ λοιδορίαν ἀντὶ λοιδορίας, “not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult” — κακός, from the evil family: harm; λοιδορία, verbal abuse, the noun of λοιδορέω in 2:23, where Christ ‘didn’t curse back’. τοὐναντίον δὲ εὐλογοῦντες, “but instead blessing” — εὐλογέω, to speak well of, to call down good. ὅτι εἰς τοῦτο ἐκλήθητε, “knowing that to this were you called” — the same calling as 2:21. ἵνα εὐλογίαν κληρονομήσητε, “that you may inherit a blessing” — bless, and you will be blessed.

scripture.text: For, “He who would love life, and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil, and his lips from speaking deceit.
scripture.understanding: Peter quotes Psalm 34:12–16. “For, ‘He who would love life, and see good days’” — θέλω, to will; ἀγαπάω, from the love family; ζωή, from the life family; εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family): to see, to experience; ἡμέρα, from the time family; ἀγαθός, from the good family. “let him keep his tongue from evil” — παύω, to stop; γλῶσσα, the tongue of James 3; κακός, from the evil family. “and his lips from speaking deceit” — χεῖλος, lips; δόλος, the deceit of 2:1 and 2:22. Peter had learned the cost of a careless tongue in the high priest's courtyard.

scripture.text: Let him turn away from evil, and do good. Let him seek peace, and pursue it.
scripture.understanding: “Let him turn away from evil, and do good” — ἐκκλίνω, to turn aside, to swerve; κακός, from the evil family, and ἀγαθός, from the good family. “Let him seek peace, and pursue it” — ζητέω, to look for; διώκω, to chase, the same verb as ‘persecute’: chase peace as hard as persecutors chase you. εἰρήνη, the wholeness of shalom.

scripture.text: For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears open to their prayer; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”
scripture.understanding: “For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears open to their prayer” — ὀφθαλμός and οὖς: God watches and listens; δίκαιος, righteous; δέησις, from the pray family: a specific petition, the word James used of powerful prayer (James 5:16). “but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” — πρόσωπον, the face turned towards in favour or against in judgement; ποιοῦντας κακά, from the evil family.

scripture.text: Now who is he who will harm you, if you become imitators of that which is good?
scripture.understanding: καὶ τίς ὁ κακώσων ὑμᾶς, “Now who is he who will harm you” — κακόω, from the evil family: to do evil to, to injure. ἐὰν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ μιμηταὶ γένησθε, “if you become imitators of that which is good?” — μιμητής, an imitator (many manuscripts read ζηλωταί, ‘zealous for’); ἀγαθός, from the good family. Generally, doing good protects; but Peter immediately admits the exception (v. 14). No one can do you ultimate harm.

scripture.text: But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. “Don’t fear what they fear, neither be troubled.”
scripture.understanding: ἀλλ᾽ εἰ καὶ πάσχοιτε διὰ δικαιοσύνην, μακάριοι, “But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed” — πάσχω, from the suffer family; δικαιοσύνη; μακάριος, the word of the Beatitudes: Jesus' words, “Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5:10). Then Isaiah 8:12: “Don’t fear what they fear, neither be troubled” — φόβος, φοβέω; ταράσσω, to stir up, agitate, as water is stirred.

scripture.text: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts; and always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear:
scripture.understanding: κύριον δὲ τὸν θεὸν ἁγιάσατε ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts” — ἁγιάζω, to set apart as holy: enthrone Him as Lord of your inner life; instead of fearing people, fear Him. The WEB follows manuscripts reading ‘the Lord God’; the earliest read κύριον τὸν Χριστόν, ‘Christ as Lord’, applying Isaiah 8:13 directly to Jesus. ἕτοιμοι ἀεὶ πρὸς ἀπολογίαν, “and always be ready to give an answer” — ἀπολογία, a defence, as in a law court. παντὶ τῷ αἰτοῦντι ὑμᾶς λόγον, “to everyone who asks you a reason” — αἰτέω, from the pray family, here ‘ask’ of people; λόγος, from the word family, here an account, a reasoned explanation. περὶ τῆς ἐν ὑμῖν ἐλπίδος, “concerning the hope that is in you” — the living hope of 1:3. μετὰ πραΰτητος καὶ φόβου, “with humility and fear” — πραΰτης, from the humble family: meekness, gentleness; φόβος towards God.

scripture.text: having a good conscience; that, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.
scripture.understanding: συνείδησιν ἔχοντες ἀγαθήν, “having a good conscience” — ἀγαθός, from the good family; συνείδησις, the inner awareness before God (2:19). ἵνα ἐν ᾧ καταλαλεῖσθε, “that, while you are spoken against” — καταλαλέω, as in 2:12. ὡς κακοποιῶν, “as evildoers” — from the evil family. καταισχυνθῶσιν, “they may be disappointed” — put to shame, the opposite of 2:6. οἱ ἐπηρεάζοντες ὑμῶν τὴν ἀγαθὴν ἐν Χριστῷ ἀναστροφήν, “who curse your good way of life in Christ” — ἐπηρεάζω, to insult, mistreat (Luke 6:28). Your answer is your words (v. 15); your proof is your life.

scripture.text: For it is better, if it is God’s will, that you suffer for doing well than for doing evil.
scripture.understanding: κρεῖττον γάρ, “For it is better” — κρείττων, the ‘better’ of Hebrews. εἰ θέλοι τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, “if it is God’s will” — θέλημα: suffering is never outside God's will for His people. πάσχειν ἀγαθοποιοῦντας ἢ κακοποιοῦντας, “that you suffer for doing well than for doing evil” — πάσχω, from the suffer family; ἀγαθοποιέω, from the good family; κακοποιέω, from the evil family. Two opposite words built on the same pattern.

scripture.text: Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God; being put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit;
scripture.understanding: ὅτι καὶ Χριστὸς ἅπαξ περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἔπαθεν, “Because Christ also suffered for sins once” — πάσχω, from the suffer family (many manuscripts read ἀπέθανεν, ‘died’); ἅπαξ, once for all, never to be repeated (Hebrews 9:28); ἁμαρτία, from the sin family. δίκαιος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων, “the righteous for the unrighteous” — substitution in four words. ἵνα ὑμᾶς προσαγάγῃ τῷ θεῷ, “that he might bring you to God” — προσάγω, to lead into the presence, as a priest leads a worshipper to the altar or a courtier brings someone before the king. θανατωθεὶς μὲν σαρκί, “being put to death in the flesh” — θανατόω; σάρξ, His human, earthly life. ζῳοποιηθεὶς δὲ πνεύματι, “but made alive in the spirit” — ζωοποιέω, from the life family: given life, in the realm of the Spirit — His resurrection life.

scripture.text: in which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison,
scripture.understanding: ἐν ᾧ καὶ τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασιν πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξεν, “in which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison” — one of the hardest verses in the New Testament. πορεύομαι, to go; φυλακή, a prison; πνεῦμα, used in the New Testament without qualification almost always of spiritual beings rather than human souls; κηρύσσω, to proclaim as a herald. The strongest reading, in light of verse 22 and 2 Peter 2:4–5, is that the risen Christ, on His way to heaven, proclaimed His victory to the rebellious spirits imprisoned since the days of Noah (Genesis 6:1–4; Jude 6). Others understand it as Christ preaching through Noah to people of his day, or preaching to the dead between His death and resurrection; Scripture nowhere teaches a second chance after death.

scripture.text: who before were disobedient, when God waited patiently in the days of Noah, while the ship was being built. In it, few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water.
scripture.understanding: ἀπειθήσασίν ποτε, “who before were disobedient” — ἀπειθέω, the word of 2:7–8 and 3:1. ὅτε ἀπεξεδέχετο ἡ τοῦ θεοῦ μακροθυμία, “when God waited patiently” — literally ‘the patience of God waited’: μακροθυμία, from the endurance family: long temper, God's refusal to give up quickly (2 Peter 3:9); ἀπεκδέχομαι, to wait eagerly. ἐν ἡμέραις Νῶε κατασκευαζομένης κιβωτοῦ, “in the days of Noah, while the ship was being built” — ἡμέρα, from the time family; κιβωτός, the ark, a great box. εἰς ἣν ὀλίγοι, τοῦτ᾽ ἔστιν ὀκτὼ ψυχαί, διεσώθησαν δι᾽ ὕδατος, “In it, few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water” — ψυχή, from the life family: persons; διασῴζω, to bring safely through. The same water that judged the world carried the ark.

scripture.text: This is a symbol of baptism, which now saves you—not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,
scripture.understanding: ὃ καὶ ὑμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σῴζει βάπτισμα, “This is a symbol of baptism, which now saves you” — ἀντίτυπος, from the pattern family: the counterpart that matches the original type. The flood is the type; baptism is the antitype. σῴζω, from the heal family: to rescue and make whole. Then Peter guards against misunderstanding: οὐ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου, “not the putting away of the filth of the flesh” — not a bath, not the ritual in itself. ἀλλὰ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς θεόν, “but the answer of a good conscience toward God” — ἀγαθός, from the good family, as in verse 16; ἐπερώτημα, a request or pledge: the formal answer given at baptism, a commitment and an appeal to God. δι᾽ ἀναστάσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” — ἀνάστασις, from the rise family: the power that saves is Christ's resurrection, received by faith and confessed in baptism.

scripture.text: who is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers being made subject to him.
scripture.understanding: ὅς ἐστιν ἐν δεξιᾷ θεοῦ, “who is at the right hand of God” — the place of honour and authority (Psalm 110:1). πορευθεὶς εἰς οὐρανόν, “having gone into heaven” — the same ‘went’ as verse 19. ὑποταγέντων αὐτῷ ἀγγέλων καὶ ἐξουσιῶν καὶ δυνάμεων, “angels and authorities and powers being made subject to him” — ὑποτάσσω, the word Peter used for believers' submission (2:13, 18; 3:1), now used of every spiritual being. ἐξουσία and δύναμις, two words from the power family: ἐξουσία, the right to rule, and δύναμις, the ability to act. Every authority and every capability in the unseen realm is under Christ.

visualMeditations.title: The Sermon Without Words
visualMeditations.image: Picture a woman in a pagan household who has become a Christian. Her husband mocks her faith, refuses to come to church and forbids her to talk about Jesus. She stops arguing. But day after day he watches: she is honest, kind, patient, unafraid. She does not dress to impress, yet there is a beauty about her he cannot explain. One evening, years later, he quietly asks, ‘Tell me about your God.’
visualMeditations.meaning: “so that, even if any don’t obey the Word, they may be won by the behavior of their wives without a word” (v. 1), “seeing your pure behavior in fear” (v. 2). The beauty that wins people is “in the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God very precious” (v. 4). Some people will never listen to your words, but they are watching your life.

visualMeditations.title: Blessing for Insult
visualMeditations.image: Picture a man insulted in public. Everyone waits for him to hit back. Instead he pauses, looks at the man who insulted him, and says, ‘May God bless you and your family.’ The crowd falls silent. The insulter does not know what to do. Above them, unseen, the eyes of the Lord are watching, and His ears are open.
visualMeditations.meaning: “not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing; knowing that to this were you called, that you may inherit a blessing” (v. 9). “For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears open to their prayer” (v. 12). Blessing your enemies is not weakness; it is trust that God sees, hears and will judge.

visualMeditations.title: Ready to Answer
visualMeditations.image: Picture a courtroom. A believer stands accused, the room hostile, the judge stern. Someone asks, ‘Why do you still have hope?’ The believer does not panic. With a calm voice and a gentle manner, she explains who Jesus is, what He has done and why her hope is alive. Her accusers have nothing to say, because her life matches her words.
visualMeditations.meaning: “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts; and always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear” (v. 15). The best defence of the faith is a heart where Christ is Lord, a mind that can explain the hope, a manner that is gentle, and a conscience that is clean (v. 16).

visualMeditations.title: The Ark and the Water
visualMeditations.image: Picture rain pouring for days, rivers bursting, the whole world sinking under water. A great wooden ship rises on the flood, and inside it eight people are safe while everything outside perishes. Then picture a river where a new believer goes down under the water and comes up again, and above the scene a risen Christ ascending to the right hand of God, with every power in the universe bowing before Him.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God” (v. 18). The flood was judgement, but it also carried Noah's family to safety. Baptism is its counterpart: not washing the body, but “the answer of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (v. 21). The One you trusted is now at God's right hand, with “angels and authorities and powers being made subject to him” (v. 22).

structure.label: Wives and Husbands (v. 1-7)
structure.body: Wives, submit to your husbands so that unbelieving husbands may be won without a word by your pure conduct; let your beauty be the inner beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, as with the holy women of old like Sarah; husbands, live with your wives with understanding, honouring them as fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers are not hindered.

structure.label: Blessing Instead of Revenge (v. 8-12)
structure.body: Be united, sympathetic, loving, compassionate and humble; do not repay evil for evil or insult for insult, but bless, for you were called to inherit a blessing; Psalm 34 promises that the Lord watches the righteous and opposes evildoers.

structure.label: Suffering for Righteousness (v. 13-17)
structure.body: Who will harm you if you are zealous for good? Even if you suffer for righteousness you are blessed; do not fear, but set apart Christ as Lord in your hearts, always ready to give a gentle and respectful defence of your hope, keeping a good conscience so that slanderers are put to shame; it is better to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.

structure.label: Christ's Suffering and Victory (v. 18-22)
structure.body: Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God; put to death in the flesh, made alive in the spirit, He proclaimed to the imprisoned spirits who disobeyed in Noah's day, when eight were saved through water; baptism, its counterpart, now saves — not by washing but as a good conscience's pledge to God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and sits at God's right hand with all angels, authorities and powers subject to Him.

sections.heading: Homes That Preach
paragraphs: Peter applies the pattern of Christ's suffering and trust (2:21–25) to marriage. He speaks first to wives, many of whom were married to unbelievers — a dangerous position in a world where a wife was expected to follow her husband's religion. Peter does not tell them to leave or to preach at their husbands. He tells them to submit, “so that, even if any don’t obey the Word, they may be won by the behavior of their wives without a word” (v. 1). A godly life is the most persuasive sermon. Paul offers the same hope: “For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7:16).

Submission here is voluntary, directed to ‘your own husband’, motivated by reverence for God, and never a call to obey commands to sin or to live in terror — “and are not put in fear by any terror” (v. 6). Its beauty is inward: “the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit” (v. 4). Gold fades and fashions change; a meek and settled spirit is precious to God forever.

Then Peter turns to husbands — remarkable in a culture that gave husbands almost total power. “You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman, as to the weaker vessel, as being also joint heirs of the grace of life” (v. 7). The wife may be physically weaker and socially more vulnerable, but before God she is a co-heir, fully equal. Paul says husbands must love their wives “even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it” (Ephesians 5:25). And Peter adds a solemn warning: the husband who dishonours his wife will find his prayers hindered. How a man treats his wife affects his relationship with God.

sections.heading: Bless, and Be Ready
paragraphs: Verse 8 widens to the whole church: “Finally, be all like-minded, compassionate, loving as brothers, tender hearted, courteous.” Three of these words come from the love and mercy families. Then comes the hardest command: “not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing” (v. 9). This is the teaching of Jesus: “love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44). Paul says the same: “Repay no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17).

Peter supports it with Psalm 34, a psalm about a man who escaped danger by God's help. The one who wants to “love life, and see good days” must guard his tongue, turn from evil, do good and chase peace (vv. 10–11). James said the tongue is a fire; Peter, who once cursed and swore in the courtyard, now quotes the psalm with deep conviction.

Even so, believers may suffer. “But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed” (v. 14). The answer to fear is a heart where Christ is enthroned: “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts; and always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear” (v. 15). This verse gives the church's whole approach to defending the faith: Christ as Lord inside, readiness to explain, a gentle and respectful manner, and a clear conscience that makes slander look foolish. Paul agrees: “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:6).

sections.heading: The Spirits in Prison and the Victory of Christ
paragraphs: Verses 18–22 begin with one of the clearest statements of the atonement in Scripture: “Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God; being put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit” (v. 18). The death was once for all. It was substitutionary — the righteous for the unrighteous. Its goal was relational — to bring you to God. And it ended in life — Christ was made alive.

Then come the most debated verses of the letter: “in which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison, who before were disobedient, when God waited patiently in the days of Noah” (vv. 19–20). Three main readings have been held. The strongest, given the word ‘spirits’ (usually used of supernatural beings), the mention of angels and powers in verse 22, and Peter's own words in 2 Peter 2:4–5, is that the risen Christ proclaimed His triumph to the rebellious spirits imprisoned since Noah's time — a herald announcing victory, not an offer of salvation. Others read it as Christ preaching through Noah to his generation, or preaching to the dead between His death and resurrection; but nowhere does Scripture offer a second chance of salvation after death, and Peter's purpose is to show Christ's total victory over every hostile power.

That victory gives meaning to baptism. Noah's family was brought safely through the water that judged the world. Baptism is its counterpart: “This is a symbol of baptism, which now saves you—not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (v. 21). Peter is careful: water does not wash away sin by itself. What saves is the risen Christ, received by faith and confessed in baptism as a believer's pledge and appeal to God. Paul says, “We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). And the chapter ends where every suffering believer needs to look: Christ “is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers being made subject to him” (v. 22).

ntConnection.heading: Christ Over Every Power
paragraphs: Peter's picture of the exalted Christ is shared by Paul. God “raised him from the dead, and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:20), “far above all rule, and authority, and power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come” (Ephesians 1:21). At the cross Christ disarmed the powers: “having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15). Peter's ‘spirits in prison’ heard the herald of that triumph.

Noah appears elsewhere as a sign of judgement and salvation. Jesus said, “As the days of Noah were, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:37). Hebrews says, “By faith, Noah, being warned about things not yet seen, moved with godly fear, prepared a ship for the saving of his house, through which he condemned the world” (Hebrews 11:7). And Peter returns to him in his second letter: God “didn’t spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah with seven others, a preacher of righteousness, when he brought a flood on the world of the ungodly” (2 Peter 2:5).

The call to answer with gentleness and to bless instead of curse is how Peter himself had to learn. In Gethsemane he drew a sword; Jesus said, “Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). Now the man who once fought with a sword teaches the church to fight with blessing, gentle answers and good lives.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “to put in proper order, i.e. decorate (literally or figuratively); specially, to snuff (a wick).” κοσμέω and its noun κόσμος originally meant ‘order, arrangement, decoration’ — the beautiful order of the universe, which is why κόσμος came to mean ‘world’. In verse 3 the WEB translates κόσμος as ‘adorning’, its original sense; our word ‘cosmetic’ comes from it. Peter does not despise beauty; he relocates it. The adornment God values is the order and beauty of a gentle, quiet, trusting heart.

Strong's: “mild, i.e. (by implication) humble.” πραΰς is meekness — strength under control, not weakness. Jesus used it of Himself: ‘gentle and humble in heart’ (Matthew 11:29). It belongs to the humble family. Paired with ἡσύχιος, ‘quiet, settled, at rest’, it describes a person who does not need to fight for position or panic under pressure, because she trusts God. Peter uses the noun πραΰτης in verse 15 for the manner of a believer's defence of the faith.

Strong's: “a plea ("apology")”. ἀπολογία was the formal speech of defence in a court of law; Paul uses it of his defence before Agrippa (Acts 26:2) and of ‘the defence of the Good News’ (Philippians 1:16). From it comes ‘apologetics’, the reasoned defence of the faith. Peter expects every believer, not only scholars, to be ready to explain the hope within them — with reasons (λόγος), but also with meekness and reverence. A cold, proud argument wins debates and loses people.

Strong's: “corresponding ("antitype"), i.e. a representative, counterpart”. ἀντίτυπος is from the pattern family: τύπος is the original impression, ἀντίτυπος the matching counterpart. Hebrews 9:24 uses it of the earthly holy place as a copy of the heavenly. Here the flood is the type and baptism its counterpart: in both, God brings His people through water that signifies judgement into new life. Baptism ‘saves’ because it is the sign and pledge of union with the risen Christ, not because water has power in itself.

Strong's: “an inquiry.” ἐπερώτημα originally meant a question or request; in later Greek it was used of the formal question and answer by which a contract was made binding. That is probably the sense here: at baptism the believer answered the question of faith — ‘Do you believe? Do you renounce evil?’ — and so made a pledge to God from a good conscience. Many translations render it ‘appeal’ or ‘pledge’. Either way, baptism is not mere washing but a personal response of faith to God.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this chapter the Holy Spirit is dealing with your closest relationships, your response to insult, and your readiness to speak about your hope.

items.title: What Is Your Home Preaching?
items.body: The Spirit asks what your spouse, your children or the people you live with see in you. Are they being won by your behaviour, or pushed away by it? Husbands: do you live with understanding and honour, or are your prayers being hindered (v. 7)? Wives: is your beauty in the hidden person of the heart (v. 4)? Single or married, ask Him what your daily conduct is saying about Christ to those closest to you.

items.title: Who Can You Bless?
items.body: Someone has insulted you or done you harm. Everything in you wants to repay it. The Spirit reminds you: “to this were you called, that you may inherit a blessing” (v. 9). Name the person. Then speak a blessing over them in prayer today — and if He leads you, in person. Watch what happens in your own heart.

items.title: Could You Explain Your Hope?
items.body: If a colleague asked you tomorrow, ‘Why do you still have hope?’, what would you say? The Spirit wants Christ enthroned in your heart and His hope ready on your lips (v. 15). Ask Him for an opportunity this week, and prepare a simple, honest answer — spoken with gentleness and respect.

audit.title: The Home Check
audit.body: Would those you live with say your faith makes you easier or harder to live with (vv. 1–7)? Is there an apology or an act of honour you owe someone at home?

audit.title: The Revenge Check
audit.body: Have you repaid evil for evil or insult for insult this month (v. 9)? In what situation do you find it hardest to bless?

audit.title: The Answer Check
audit.body: Could you explain in two minutes why you believe in Jesus and what your hope is (v. 15)? When you do speak about your faith, is it with gentleness and respect, or with pride and anger?

practices.title: Write Your Two-Minute Answer
practices.body: This week, write down your answer to the question ‘What is the hope in you?’ in no more than 300 words: who Jesus is, what He has done for you, and why your hope is alive. Read it aloud until you can say it naturally. Then pray for one person to ask you, and be ready.

practices.title: Seven Days of Blessing
practices.body: For seven days, every time someone irritates, insults or mistreats you, respond with a silent prayer of blessing for them, and at least once with a spoken word of kindness. Keep a short record. At the end of the week, read verses 8–12 again and thank God for what He did in you.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, You suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring me to God. Thank You that You were put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit, and that You now sit at the right hand of God with angels, authorities and powers subject to You. Let my home preach You. Make my conduct pure and reverent, my beauty that of a gentle and quiet spirit, and my love honouring and understanding, so that my prayers are not hindered. Make me like-minded, compassionate, loving, tender-hearted and humble. When I am insulted, give me grace not to insult back but to bless, for I was called to inherit a blessing. Guard my tongue from evil and my lips from deceit; help me turn from evil, do good, and chase after peace. When I suffer for doing right, let me know that I am blessed and not be afraid. I set You apart as Lord in my heart. Make me ready to give an answer to everyone who asks about the hope within me, with gentleness and respect and a good conscience. Thank You for the salvation You gave me through Your resurrection, and for the pledge I made to You in baptism. Keep me faithful to it. In Your name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: Sarah, Daughter of Hope
storyConnections.summary: Sarah followed Abraham from Ur to an unknown land, endured years of barrenness, and twice was put in danger by her husband's fear. When the Lord promised her a son in her old age, she laughed to herself, saying, ‘After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?’ — and Peter notes that even then she called him ‘lord’. Yet her hope was not finally in Abraham but in God, who kept His promise and gave her Isaac. Peter tells believing women that they are her daughters when they do good and are not terrified by fear: their trust, like hers, rests in God.

storyConnections.title: Noah Builds the Ark
storyConnections.summary: When the earth was filled with violence, God told Noah to build an ark and warned of a coming flood. For years Noah built while the world mocked, and God waited patiently. Then the rain came, the fountains of the deep burst open, and the waters covered the earth. Only eight people — Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives — were brought safely through the water. The same flood that judged the world lifted the ark. Peter sees in it a picture of baptism: passing through the water of judgement into new life, saved by God's provision.

storyConnections.title: Peter's Sword in the Garden
storyConnections.summary: When the soldiers came to arrest Jesus in Gethsemane, Peter drew his sword and cut off the ear of the high priest's servant, Malchus. Jesus stopped him: “Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52), and healed the man's ear. Peter had tried to defend Jesus by force; within hours he was denying Him with curses. Now, years later, the same Peter writes that believers must not repay evil for evil, but bless, and must defend their hope with words spoken in gentleness and respect. He had learned that the kingdom is not defended with a sword.
